title: No compulsion
hookLine: let there be no compulsion in religion (Quran 2:256)
tomorrow: Guru Nanak went into a river and didn't come out. then what?

cards: Across a holiday table, one relative leans on another: just believe what I believe. That isn't really an argument anymore. Yesterday's question was whether anyone can be made to.
The Quran answers in its second surah: "There is no compulsion in religion." And there's a story behind the line.
A report from Ibn Abbas, in Abu Dawud's collection, says that before Islam, some women of Medina whose babies kept dying would vow that if a child lived, they'd raise it Jewish.
Later, when the Jewish tribe of Banu Nadir was sent out of Medina, some of those children were among them, and their Muslim relatives said: we won't let our children go. Then the verse came.

teach.h: READING ONE: A RULE FOR EVERYONE.
teach.b: Here's the debate, and Muslim scholars have stood on both sides of it. The first reading: this is a rule for everyone.
Belief lives in the heart, and the verse goes on to say that the right way has become clear from error.
Forced faith isn't faith, so no one may be forced. Read this way, the Medina story is one case of a wide law.

teach.h: READING TWO: A RULING WITH AN OCCASION.
teach.b: The second reading, recorded by early commentators such as al-Tabari: the verse was a ruling about particular people at a particular time, and other verses and rulings shaped how far it reached. Its best case is serious.
Read a law with its occasion. A ruling given about certain children isn't automatically a ruling about everything.
Al-Tabari sets out several of these views side by side, and they all start from the same verse.
So the verse itself is plain: there is no compulsion in religion. What Muslims have argued about, carefully, is how far that line reaches.
A detail to keep: this verse comes right after the Throne Verse, a passage on God's power and care.

how: Muslim scholars and teachers discuss Quran 2:256 in commentary and law, alongside its occasion in the hadith and the verses around it.

practice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms open and turned up. Bring to mind one person whose path is different from yours, and keep the hands open while you hold them there: no grip, no pull. Let the breath come and go on its own.
